chunk_findings.detail: The added block is emitted with bare control tags and no whitespace control (`{%- ... -%}`). Under Jinja2's default whitespace settings (`trim_blocks=False`, `lstrip_blocks=False`), the newline that follows a block tag is literal text. The old template went straight from the `#}` comment line to `{% if adopted %}`, so exactly one literal newline preceded the adopted section. The new template inserts `{% endif %}\n` between them: for the default `[mcp].tools = all` case `tier_note(tier, names=False)` yields `""`, the `if` body is skipped, but the newline after `{% endif %}` is still emitted, so the rendered `instructions` string acquires one extra `\n` (an extra blank line) before the `{% if adopted %}` content compared with today. Given input `[mcp].tools` unset (default `all`), the `initialize` response at `mcp.py:3038` therefore returns instructions that are not byte-identical to the previous release, violating the acceptance criterion; a byte-for-byte comparison of the default-tier handshake instructions fails. (The truthy branch has the same issue in reverse — the newline after `{% if tool_tier_note %}` is inside the body, so a non-`all` tier gets a leading blank line plus three trailing newlines after the note.) This only holds if the renderer does not enable `trim_blocks`; the tags as written rely entirely on that setting.

chunk_findings.detail: These tests never clear `DDFLOW_MCP_TOOLS`; they take no `monkeypatch` (or ignore it) and rely on the ambient environment being unset. The change itself establishes that this variable overrides the config at `Server` construction. So with a plain `DDFLOW_MCP_TOOLS=core` exported in the shell/CI (a very plausible state for anyone trying the knob the README now documents), `_list(repo)` returns only `CORE_TOOLS` while `expected` in `test_default_is_all_and_byte_identical_to_the_unfiltered_list` is built from the full `TOOLS`, and the equality assertion fails; likewise `assert Server(repo).tier == "core"` fails if the ambient value is `all`/`standard`, and the tier is no longer `all`, so the help text mentions the tier and `test_help_says_nothing_about_tiers_at_all` fails too. The fix is an autouse fixture doing `monkeypatch.delenv("DDFLOW_MCP_TOOLS", raising=False)` so these tests assert the default rather than the developer's environment.

chunk_findings.detail: The callability half of this test does not actually verify the property the change promises ("a tool outside the tier is still CALLABLE"). It only asserts `"unknown tool" not in json.dumps(called)`, which is a single failure phrase. If the tier filter regressed the call path in any other way — e.g. the server answered with `{"isError": true, "content": [{"text": "tool 'ddflow_loops' is not available in the 'core' tier"}]}` — the assertion still passes, because that string does not contain "unknown tool". The test should assert the call succeeded (result present, no `isError`, and/or the same non-error output produced when the tier is `all`), otherwise it cannot detect the exact regression it was written to guard against.

data.title: tests/test_mcp_tool_tiers.py :: test_hidden_tool_is_still_callable_and_named_by_help

chunk_findings.detail: The new equality assertion assumes that calling `ddflow_loops` twice — once on the server constructed in the `core` tier and once on a freshly constructed server in the `all` tier — yields byte-identical `result` dicts. The tier is a property of the *listing*, not of the *call*; the intent explicitly only guarantees that a tool outside the tier "is still CALLABLE ... so nothing breaks" and that `ddflow_help` names the rest. It never states that a hidden tool's output is invariant across tiers. Any tier-dependent detail carried in a tool result (a hint/marker noting the tool is outside the tier, a per-instance seed/id, or a timestamp/relative-time field emitted by the tool wrapper) makes this assertion fail even though the feature is implemented correctly. The test worked before precisely because it only checked `"unknown tool" not in json.dumps(called)`, i.e. that the tool was *routed*, not that its output matched another tier's. If the server is stateful per call (the first call mutating loop/session state that the second call then reports), the comparison also diverges for reasons unrelated to the tier. Because the assertion pins a property (output identity across tiers) that the stated acceptance criteria do not require, it can produce a false failure; it should instead compare only the properties that matter (e.g. that both calls succeed), which the preceding `assert not called.get("isError")` already does.
